VAT- An increase in the cost of living

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With the majority of South Africans living below the poverty line, the recent increase in VAT by 1% will increase the cost of living. How will the poor compensate from their already empty pockets?

Unique Selling Point:
For the first time in 25 years government has imposed a new VAT increase from 14% to 15%. Given the state of the country some believe tampering with tax was a necessary but it’s the poor and vulnerable households that will feel the effect of an increase in the cost of living.

Summary:
According to StatsSA poverty trends show the number of people falling into poverty has risen to about 55.5% in the country. 1 in 4 people in South Africa are living below the amount necessary to keep alive as many get to survive on less. While unemployment is soaring at 36% and about 45%, almost half of the country’s population is dependent on social grants. This is a clear assault on the poor.
Pro- poor organizations and workers unions are up in arms with the minister’s budget speech highlighting that there isn’t enough done to help the poor, which are the majority in this country, to cope with the VAT increases. The number of zero-rated food items is not enough according to the Cosatu. Cosatu also believe all food, water and electricity should be zero rated and they are willing to strike for it. Similarly the SPII believes that buying power is being taken away from the already struggling vulnerable households in the country. According to PACSA people can not survive on zero rated food items alone as it not enough for an adequate nutritional diet. The Cost of living will get unbearable as it will not just be food and basic household items that will go up but transport, which is a daily need for many South Africans will be affected.
Carte Blanche will highlight this through a trolley run in a supermarket. With a child support grant budget, we’ll fill the trolley up with zero-rated food items and a nutritional basket to emphasize how much buying power has been taken from the consumer.

Further information:
On the 21st of February 2018 Malusi Gigaba, the then Finance Minister of South Africa, delivered a budget speech that was largely viewed as anti-poor and designed to further entrench South Africans into poverty. The increase by 1% on Value Added Tax to 15% coupled with the 52% fuel levy will only make the cost of living for millions of South Africans. Even though economist and some quarters of the economy had anticipated for treasury to temper with tax, some believe it was necessary, but the increase by a percentage point will still affect the poor and the working class heavily. The tax hikes are part of a package of measures to raise an additional R36-billion in light of a revenue gap of R48.2-billion in the current year.

The Minister suggested that an above average increase of social grants is meant to alleviate the sting of the new VAT. What the government conveniently neglects however is that an increase of 6.6% for child grants matched against 5.5% inflation increase in 2018 amounts to a mere 1.1%. Zero-rated food items such as Maize, brown bread, beans, etc are also seen as an option for the poor to deal with the VAT increase, but living on these items does not come close to a balanced nutritional diet.

The bottom line is that VAT is here, though some believe is the government’s way of making the public pay for their own misdeeds through corruption and mismanagement of funds, some see it as a necessary implementation given the state of the country’s fiscus. However, the fact is, its the poor that will carry the burden the most. A mere 1% increase will add to the cost of living for all South Africans, but how hard will it hit on the pockets of the poor and the middle class? Carte Blanche finds out.

Press Release:


Value Added Tax will be increased to 15% from 1 April 2018. Some say it’s a necessary step to keep the economy on track, but others blame it squarely on State capture and corruption. The big question is: with the majority of South Africans living below the poverty line, how will the poor compensate from their already empty pockets?

Script:



Dlamini: South Africa cannot survive the increase on vat

Trinity: for me it’s like blackmail, its ransom - we don't have the money so we have to get it from somewhere

Isobel: The poor are supporting the developmental needs we have and they’re the ones that need assistance from the fiscus.

Link: 17 Million South Africans live on social grants. Unemployment is at a high. With an increase on VAT to 15% from the 1st of April, is this the most anti-poor legislation since the dawn of democracy.


Gigaba: The tax proposals for the 2018 budget are designed to generate an additional R 36 bn.The main tax proposals are: an increase in the value-added tax rate from 14 to 15 percent ...

VO: Sdumo Dlamini COSATU President, believes the country is heading for a disaster.

Dlamini: You are now adding this expense on the poor. What is happening is what we calling a time ticking bomb of the poor. They going to be rising up looking for all of us in our big high walls, they will wait for us at the gate to give in to their demand. And that is not what we want as a country, a revolt.

VO: 12.1 million children receive the child support grant. For the majority of mothers this is their only reliable source of monthly income, currently at R380 per month, which is way below the food poverty line of R531 per capita and even further below the cost which allows mothers to feed their children a basic nutritious diet.

VOX POP - Lydia Mofokeng: When it comes to how much I spend right now on food, I don't know because I just buy what I can afford just so we can survive until month end. When the VAT hits it’s going to be worse

VO: Isobel Frye Director of Studies in Poverty and Inequality Institute says that even though social grants will be increased this will barely scratch the surface of what the poor need.

Isobel: We were told 5.5% increase in pensions and 6.6% increase in child support grants but if you deduct the cost of living inflation what you are looking at is a 1.1% increase and a 0. 4% increase so effectively the 1% increase in vat rules out the benefits that those social grants can take.

VOX POP - Nonhlanhla Shasha: It is a bad thing really, what about people those who are not working and those who are getting pension money… really it’s going to be tough.

VO: So why are the poor so significant when we talk of a VAT increase? The facts are glaringly devastating. According to the latest Stats SA Report, cycles of poverty are now escalating and accelerating. Doctor Julie Smith, heads research and advocacy for the Pietermaritzburg Agency for Community Social Action. PACSA.

Julie: The current unemployment for black SA is sitting at 30% but the expanded unemployment rate for black SA is at 40.7%. The medium wage currently for black SA is R2 900 and you disperse it into a family of 4 people and you get to a figure of 725 rand a month that is below the upper bound poverty line of R 1 138 and that really is a context that we need to see the vat hike.

VO: Over 80% of state revenue comes from personal income tax, corporate income tax and VAT. With a revenue gap of 48.2 Billion Rands an increase of VAT to 15% could raise about 20 Billion rands for the national purse. Judge Dennis Davis is chair of the Davis Tax Commission.

Davis: If we hadn't had that VAT increase we would have essentially, probably been downgraded even further, probably would have gotten greater interest cost which would have effectively meant lesser money for social reconstruction and i'm afraid to say as hard as this is we had to find the money to plug the gap.

Nhlanhla: Well corruption was an aspect contributing to this VAt increase would you agree?
Davis: We are paying for ten years of an eroding base of integrity and accountability and increasing levels of corruption both in the public and we must never forget in the private sector, which is equally culpable in this regard.

VO: Judge Davis says other factors that contributed to the shortfall were, low economic growth and a decline of SARS’s tax revenue collection. Economist Trinity Ncube, believes government spending is another major contributor.

Trinity: The deficit has come from as a result of budget spending being more than the tax revenue, just a bloated government and deputies which people do not add value to the economy. Of course another wastage is in municipalities and when you hear all these corrupt activities that happen.

Davis: Wasted expenditure is not necessarily fraudulent but it's wasted.If we reduce that by say 30% we probably wouldn't have needed the VAT increase.

VOX POP - Rethabile Nonkonyana:
0001OF.mov[10:42:59.21] Rethabile: Already I feel like is affecting us even before is goes upcustomers are not as many like before. I already had to let go of one because of this VAT thing.

LINK: Food is a basic necessity for millions of South African families. An increase in VAT means a decrease in buying power.

Isobel: The poor people the one thing you can change is food your rental stays the same transport stays the same your other costs stay the same so what poor people have to do is eat less.

Julie: A lot of the foods that we have here are a representation of the foods that PACSA track and its useful here to differentiate what foods are zero rated and which foods are vatable.

VO: The poor spend between 60 and 70 percent of their income on food, so many argue that all food should be exempt from VAT, or at least there should be more zero rated foods than the current list of 19 items, especially since the zero rated foods are not necessarily the cheapest or the most economical.

Julie: So pilchards is one of the only protein that is zero in the basket. The problem is that it’s very expensive and households need more than one or two tins for a meal.

VO: Milk is zero rated, but is often replaced with powdered milk which is vated, because it stretches further.

Julie: Kids crave protein and if a mother turns her back for half a second the milk has disappeared.

VO: The other zero rated proteins are beans and eggs which need to be cooked. Electricity is a vatable expense.

Julie: With a sandwich the only thing that is not vatable are your two slices of brown bread

Dlamini: The last time we had a discussion which of the types of food that need to be zero rated would have been during the apartheid government, have we gone back to check the list?

Nhlanhla: Let’s talk about the zero rated food items how are they selected

Julie: We are not clear on how they were selected we are clear that somebody selected them for somebody else. When you look at the zero rated food items it doesn't include all of the foods people buy and need to live at a dignified level for example there, aren’t any meat products.

VO: PACSA Tracks a basket of 38 basic foods which women say they try and buy for their families each month

Nhlanhla: How much buying power is cut

Julie: It’s going to contribute R 222 to a basket of R3 113 so around 7%. It’s going to have an implication directly on the nutrition of households

VO: And the austerity measures on the budget did not stop at a one percentage point increase on VAT, which in real terms is a 7% increase of VAT.

Upsound Gigaba speech on the 52 cents fuel levy

VOX POP - Nonhlanhla Shasha I’m spending for petrol only three thousand rands, so it’s going to be 3.6 maybe a month it’s too much really, and it’s not only petrol.


Trinity: The fuel levy is actually more damaging than the vat. We are talking almost 11% increase in the cost of everything that’s going to come in and that’s going to feed into the inflation process of everything else that has to be transported which is pretty much everything you buy in a shop there is going to be an increase all of that

VO: Some economists believe that the combined effect of the Vat increase and the fuel levy will decrease purchasing power by up to 20%

Trinity: We are going to see people spending less on R100 than before and that 100 may now be worth 80 now that has a ripple effect into the economy.
VO: 20% for middle class earners on R16 500 per month, will see them lose R3300 of their buying power and already notifications of price rises are arriving in consumers’ inboxes, everything from water, electricity, data, medical expenses and the like, will be affected.

VOX POP - Nonhlanhla Shasha: I won't manage really, I won't manage at all

Link: Labour organisations and civil society are standing united against this hike. They’re not going to take it lying down.


Dlamini: We want the anc in their manifesto to declare that this vat thing is not going to fly. we are building up to a huge mass action in this country.

Davis: I think that we're probably going to find that there will be further zero ratings to soften the impact for poorer people and rightfully so.

VO: Ultimately the fate of the South African economy seems to lie in how the poor and destitute are uplifted.

Trinity: So the capacity to tax comes from having more people involved in the economy, there is a dire need to create jobs you have more people come in then you have a larger tax base in that case it makes sense to then start taxing a lot of people even if you increase the vat by 0.5% 1%.

FIN!!!!!!!!!!
PROMO 1: 15”

VO: Is government plunging millions of South Africans further into poverty in an attempt to recoup its mismanaged funds?

Davis: As hard as this is we had to find the money to plug the gap.



PROMO 2. 15”

VO: An increase of one percentage point to VAT in April and a 52 cents hike on the fuel levy leaves South Africans 20 percent poorer.

Trinity: The fuel levy is actually more damaging than the vat.


PROMO 10”

VO: With mounting government deficit, Treasury is banking on VAT to recover revenue. But can South Africans tolerate what amounts to an extra 20% burden on their budgets?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With the majority of South Africans living below the poverty line, the recent increase in VAT by 1% will increase the cost of living. How will the poor compensate from their already empty pockets?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: For the first time in 25 years government has imposed a new VAT increase from 14% to 15%. Given the state of the country some believe tampering with tax was a necessary but it’s the poor and vulnerable households that will feel the effect of an increase in the cost of living.
metadata.Summary: According to StatsSA poverty trends show the number of people falling into poverty has risen to about 55.5% in the country. 1 in 4 people in South Africa are living below the amount necessary to keep alive as many get to survive on less. While unemployment is soaring at 36% and about 45%, almost half of the country’s population is dependent on social grants. This is a clear assault on the poor. Pro- poor organizations and workers unions are up in arms with the minister’s budget speech highlighting that there isn’t enough done to help the poor, which are the majority in this country, to cope with the VAT increases. The number of zero-rated food items is not enough according to the Cosatu. Cosatu also believe all food, water and electricity should be zero rated and they are willing to strike for it. Similarly the SPII believes that buying power is being taken away from the already struggling vulnerable households in the country. According to PACSA people can not survive on zero rated food items alone as it not enough for an adequate nutritional diet. The Cost of living will get unbearable as it will not just be food and basic household items that will go up but transport, which is a daily need for many South Africans will be affected. Carte Blanche will highlight this through a trolley run in a supermarket. With a child support grant budget, we’ll fill the trolley up with zero-rated food items and a nutritional basket to emphasize how much buying power has been taken from the consumer.
metadata.Further information: On the 21st of February 2018 Malusi Gigaba, the then Finance Minister of South Africa, delivered a budget speech that was largely viewed as anti-poor and designed to further entrench South Africans into poverty. The increase by 1% on Value Added Tax to 15% coupled with the 52% fuel levy will only make the cost of living for millions of South Africans. Even though economist and some quarters of the economy had anticipated for treasury to temper with tax, some believe it was necessary, but the increase by a percentage point will still affect the poor and the working class heavily. The tax hikes are part of a package of measures to raise an additional R36-billion in light of a revenue gap of R48.2-billion in the current year. The Minister suggested that an above average increase of social grants is meant to alleviate the sting of the new VAT. What the government conveniently neglects however is that an increase of 6.6% for child grants matched against 5.5% inflation increase in 2018 amounts to a mere 1.1%. Zero-rated food items such as Maize, brown bread, beans, etc are also seen as an option for the poor to deal with the VAT increase, but living on these items does not come close to a balanced nutritional diet. The bottom line is that VAT is here, though some believe is the government’s way of making the public pay for their own misdeeds through corruption and mismanagement of funds, some see it as a necessary implementation given the state of the country’s fiscus. However, the fact is, its the poor that will carry the burden the most. A mere 1% increase will add to the cost of living for all South Africans, but how hard will it hit on the pockets of the poor and the middle class? Carte Blanche finds out.
